1289.title: The kirpan and the law
1289.hook: many countries' laws make space for the kirpan
1289.howItsDone: Initiated Sikhs wear the kirpan sheathed, usually on a cloth strap under their clothes, and in many countries the law allows it, often with conditions on size or how it is worn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, styles of turban: the pagg, the patka, the keski, the tall dumalla. Your line was many styles, one crown.

A security line. Trays, belts, keys, the beep of the scanner. A man in a turban steps up and quietly tells the officer he's wearing a kirpan, a small curved blade, sheathed, under his shirt on a cloth strap. The officer pauses. There's a rulebook somewhere for this moment, and both of them are hoping the other one knows it. It happens at school gates, courthouse doors, office lobbies and arenas. Early on, this path asked: is that a knife? Today, what happens when an article of faith meets a rule written for everyone.
screen: `A SECURITY LINE.` → `I'M WEARING A KIRPAN.` → `FAITH MEETS A RULE FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Start with the faith side. The kirpan is one of the five Ks, the articles the Sikh code asks the initiated to keep on the body. It's usually worn in a sheath, on a cloth strap across the body, often under the clothes. Sikhs speak of it as a sign of the duty to protect the weak and stand against injustice: a reminder, not a tool for a quarrel. An initiated Sikh doesn't take it off for convenience; it's part of who they've promised to be. Now the law side. Laws about blades are written to keep people safe, and they usually don't have a kirpan in mind. When the two meet, someone has to work out how to honor both. Laws in a number of places make space for the kirpan, in different ways. Some name religious articles directly. Some allow it with conditions, such as its size, a sheath, or wearing it under clothing. Some places, such as aircraft cabins, often still say no, and Sikhs find other ways, sometimes with a small symbolic kirpan. Courts in more than one country have weighed these questions, and the answers change as laws change. What doesn't change is the shape of the problem. A Sikh is asking: may I keep my promise here? The law is asking: can everyone here be safe? A good rule tries to answer yes to both.

segments.voice: Hold the question gently: where you live, what might the rule be for a kirpan at a school, a courthouse, an airport, and how sure do you feel? Then picture both people in that security line, the Sikh and the officer, each trying to do the right thing. Wish them both a good answer.
The kirpan and the law. An article of faith worn by initiated Sikhs, and the laws in many countries that make space for it, often with conditions. Today's word.

1290.title: Kara and kangha, daily
1290.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the five Ks wear a plain steel kara on the wrist and keep a small kangha in the hair every day, and Sikhs often describe them as reminders of the Guru's way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kirpan and the law: a promise and a rule meeting at a security line. Your line was faith and law.

A string tied around a finger. A sticky note on the fridge. An alarm with a label. People lean on small things to hold big intentions, because big intentions slip away by lunchtime. Watch a Sikh at a kitchen counter, reaching for a knife to cut vegetables, and you might catch the light on a plain steel band at the wrist. At the end of the day you might see a small comb tucked into the knot of hair. Two of the five Ks are small enough to forget you're wearing them. Sikhs wear them so they won't forget.
screen: `A STRING AROUND A FINGER.` → `A STEEL BAND AT THE WRIST.` → `SMALL ENOUGH TO FORGET.`

segments.voice: Start with the kara. It's a plain bracelet, usually of steel or iron, worn on the wrist by Sikhs who keep the five Ks, and by other Sikhs too. It isn't jewelry: no gold, no gems, no clasp. Early on this path, it came with a question: what are these hands doing? Sikhs often point to two things about it. Its shape is a circle, with no beginning and no end, which they take as a reminder of the One without beginning or end. And its place is the wrist, right where the hand begins. Before the hand takes, strikes, signs or gives, it passes the kara: a small steel question on the way. Is this an act the Guru would stand behind? Now the kangha. You met it a few days ago as a tool of care. Today, see it as a reminder. It lives in the hair all day, a quiet sign that a Sikh life is meant to be kept in order, clean and tended, not tangled and neglected. Some Sikhs pair the two in their own way: a touch of the kara before work, a moment with the kangha at night. Neither is magic. The code rejects charms and lucky objects, as you heard earlier on this path. The kara and the kangha protect no one by themselves; they work only when they're noticed. That's why they're worn every day. A reminder you see once a year is a decoration. A reminder on your wrist all day is a practice.

segments.voice: Rest the fingers of one hand on the other wrist: if you wear a kara, feel the cool steel; if not, feel your pulse, or just the bone. Picture the next thing your hands will do, pick up a phone, open a door, hold someone, and ask quietly whether it's something you'd stand behind. Stay there, fingers on your wrist, and breathe.

1291.title: Food and the code
1291.hook: the code forbids ritually slaughtered meat; many Sikhs are vegetarian, others not
1291.howItsDone: Initiated Sikhs do not eat kutha, ritually slaughtered meat; some Sikhs are vegetarian and others eat other meat, and gurdwara langar is served vegetarian so that everyone can share it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kara and kangha: a steel circle at the wrist and a comb in the hair. Your line was touch and remember.

Two Sikh households, same street, same gurdwara. In one kitchen there hasn't been meat for as long as anyone can remember; the grandmother says it simply isn't their way. In the other, there's chicken on the stove for dinner. On Sunday morning both families sit side by side in the langar hall and eat the same meal: dal, a vegetable dish, roti and a sweet. Nobody at the table asks what's waiting at home. What does the Sikh code actually say about food? Less than some expect, and the little it says matters.
screen: `TWO KITCHENS, ONE STREET.` → `THE SAME LANGAR MEAL.` → `WHAT DOES THE CODE SAY?`

segments.voice: First, the line it draws. Among the things an initiated Sikh must never do, which you met early on this path, the code names eating kutha: meat from an animal killed by ritual slaughter. Sikhs explain it in more than one way. Some see it as refusing to take part in another community's rite; others, as one piece of the Sikh refusal of empty ritual. Either way, it's a firm line. Second, what the code leaves open. It doesn't say every Sikh must be vegetarian, so Sikhs differ. Some keep a vegetarian kitchen, and some groups within the panth hold to it strictly and with deep feeling. Others eat meat that isn't kutha. Both families on that street can be keeping the code. Third, the shared table. The langar serves vegetarian food so that anyone, whatever their own rules about food, can sit and share it. The Guru's kitchen chooses the meal that leaves no one out. Fourth, the Guru Granth Sahib itself. In a hymn of Guru Nanak at Ang twelve eighty-nine, the Guru says, in paraphrase, that fools argue about flesh and meat while knowing nothing of meditation and spiritual wisdom. Some readers take it as a warning not to make food the measure of holiness; others read it alongside their own vegetarian practice and find no conflict. The code draws one line about what goes on the plate. The hymn asks about the one eating.

segments.voice: If you have something to eat or drink nearby, even a sip of water, look at it first and think of the hands it passed through: a farmer, a driver, a cook. Then take one small bite or sip, slowly, and notice the taste, the texture, the warmth or the cool. If you pray, remember the Giver as you eat.

1292.title: Why no intoxicants
1292.hook: a clear mind is kept for remembrance
1292.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the Rehat Maryada abstain from alcohol, tobacco and other intoxicants, and amritdhari Sikhs are told at initiation never to use tobacco.

segments.voice: Yesterday, food and the code: one firm line, and a table that leaves no one out. Your line was eat mindfully.

A wedding reception, late. The music is loud, the tables crowded, and a tray of drinks comes around for the third time. One guest in a turban smiles, shakes his head, and asks for another glass of lime soda. Nobody makes a fuss. His cousin says it the way you'd mention someone's shoe size: he's amritdhari, he doesn't drink. That's how the rule often gets met: a no. But a rule seen only from the outside can look like a wall. What is this one protecting?
screen: `A TRAY OF DRINKS, A THIRD TIME.` → `LIME SODA, PLEASE.` → `WHAT IS THE RULE PROTECTING?`

segments.voice: The code is plain. The Sikh Rehat Maryada tells a Sikh not to take alcohol, tobacco or other intoxicants, and tobacco is named again among the four things the initiated must never do, which you met early on this path. The reason sits in the Guru Granth Sahib. In a short verse by Guru Amar Das on Ang 554, a person pours a drink, it goes down, and, in paraphrase, understanding leaves, confusion comes in, and the drinker can no longer tell what is his own from what belongs to someone else. Then the verse turns: don't drink this false drink if you can help it, and look for a different one. The Gurus don't only say no to one kind of drink; they talk about another. In a hymn by Guru Nanak on Ang 360, a distillery becomes a picture of the spiritual life: make wisdom the raw sugar, meditation the flowers, good deeds the bark, and the result is a wine of the Name. Some readers call this the other intoxication, being soaked through with the remembrance of God. Now the wedding makes sense. A clear mind is kept for remembrance: the morning prayers, the Name repeated, the eyes open to God in other people. Anything that clouds the mind clouds that. So the no isn't only a no. It's a yes to staying awake. And it's no judgment on the table, either. The rule is about what a Sikh keeps clear in themselves, not about who else is holding a glass.
screen: `THE CODE: NO ALCOHOL, NO TOBACCO.` · `ANG 554: UNDERSTANDING LEAVES.` · `ANG 360: A WINE OF THE NAME.` · then, large: `A CLEAR MIND, KEPT FOR REMEMBRANCE.`

segments.voice: If a glass of water is close by, hold it up and notice how the light comes through, how you can see straight through it to the other side. Then set it down and let the breath come and go, noticing how clear your own mind is right now, cloudy in places, bright in others, no grading. If you pray, let the word Waheguru ride on the breath.

Why no intoxicants. The code forbids alcohol, tobacco and other intoxicants, and the Gurus give the reason: the mind is kept clear for remembrance, and the only intoxication worth having is the Name. Today's word.

1293.title: Faithfulness in marriage
1293.hook: fidelity in marriage as part of rehat
1293.howItsDone: The Sikh Rehat Maryada asks Sikhs to be faithful to their spouse, and at amrit initiates are told that adultery is one of four things they must never do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why no intoxicants: one wine refused, and another, the Name, offered. Your line was clear mind.

A ring on a kitchen windowsill, set down while someone does the dishes. A kara on a wrist, never taken off at all. Two small circles, two kinds of promise. Most of the Sikh code has looked outward: what to wear, eat and drink, how to bow. Today's rule lives somewhere quieter: at home, between two people, on ordinary days when nobody else is watching. The code names faithfulness in marriage as part of a Sikh's rehat. Why does a code about turbans and prayers reach into a marriage?
screen: `A RING ON A WINDOWSILL.` → `A KARA ON A WRIST.` → `A RULE THAT LIVES AT HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. The Rehat Maryada asks a Sikh to keep to their own spouse and to look on others with respect: in paraphrase, a man is to regard another's wife as his mother or sister, and a woman another's husband as her father or brother. Adultery is named among the four things the initiated must never do, on the same short list as cutting the hair and using tobacco. That placement says something: for a Sikh who has taken amrit, faithfulness is as much a part of the vow as the kesh. Second, the picture behind it. In a verse by Guru Amar Das on Ang 788, in paraphrase: they are not husband and wife who merely sit together; they are husband and wife who are one light in two bodies. A marriage isn't two people sharing a house. It's one light living in two forms. Third, the portrait of a good life in the Sukhmani Sahib, on Ang 274, includes eyes that don't dwell on another's spouse. Faithfulness starts small, with where the eyes rest, long before anything happens. Fourth, notice how it fits the Anand Karaj, the wedding you met earlier in this block. The couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib together, and the hymns of that walk are about the soul's marriage to God. Some readers hear the two marriages leaning on each other: keeping faith with a spouse as practice for keeping faith with God, and the other way around. On that reading, the vow at home and the vow to the Guru are the same kind of promise.
screen: `ADULTERY: ONE OF THE FOUR AVOIDED.` · `ANG 788: ONE LIGHT IN TWO BODIES.` · `ANG 274: WHERE THE EYES REST.` · then, large: `TWO MARRIAGES, ONE PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one promise you've made to someone you live with or love: a vow, or something small, like I'll call on Sundays, or I'll be home by six. Notice how it's going, without scolding yourself. Then choose one small way to keep it, and let that settle into the breath.

1294.title: Rehat as love
1294.hook: rules kept from love, not fear
1294.howItsDone: Some Sikh teachers describe the rehat as a way of loving the Guru, and point to Guru Nanak's line on Ang 1412 about playing the game of love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faithfulness in marriage: one light in two bodies. Your line was faithful.

Every evening, in one house, a teenager practices a piano piece because a parent is standing in the doorway with a timer. In the house next door, another teenager practices the same piece because she heard it once on a rainy afternoon and can't get it out of her head. From the hallway, they sound almost the same: same scales, same wrong notes, same hour. Ask each of them in ten years whether they still play, and you'll likely hear two very different answers. A code can be kept the first way. Did the Gurus mean it to be kept the second?
screen: `TWO STUDENTS, ONE PIECE.` → `ONE HAS A TIMER IN THE DOORWAY.` → `ONE CAN'T GET THE TUNE OUT OF HER HEAD.`

segments.voice: Begin with the Japji, at its twenty-first step, on Ang 4. Guru Nanak names three things together: hearing, believing, and holding love in the mind. In paraphrase, the one who hears, accepts and loves bathes at a shrine deep inside. The order matters. Hearing comes first, and love is where it lands. Then a line from Guru Nanak on Ang 1412, in paraphrase: if you want to play the game of love, come to my lane with your head on your palm. That's not a soft line. It asks for everything. But it calls the asking a game of love, not a duty roster. Now, honestly: the Gurus also speak of bhau, a word for fear, or awe, of God, and the Japji itself talks about it. Some readers hear awe in it more than terror, the feeling of standing before something vast. Love and awe sit side by side in the hymns, without one canceling the other. But it's love the Gurus call a game, and love they ask to be played. So read the rehat that way. The kesh, the morning banis, the clear mind, faithfulness at home: they can be kept with someone standing in the doorway, a parent, a community, a worry about what people will say. Or they can be kept the way the second student plays, because the tune is already inside. The code itself can't tell the difference from the hallway. Only the one keeping it knows.
screen: `ANG 4: HEARING, BELIEVING, LOVING.` · `ANG 1412: THE GAME OF LOVE.` · `BHAU: AWE BESIDE LOVE.` · then, large: `THE SAME RULE, KEPT TWO WAYS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one rule you already keep, a habit, a promise, a line you won't cross, and ask gently why you keep it: is someone standing in the doorway, or is there a tune you love underneath? There's no wrong answer. Then hold that rule as something you'd choose again today, and let the breath be easy.
Rehat as love. The Gurus put love at the end of hearing and believing, and call the whole path a game of love. The rules can be kept from fear or from love; the hymns point to love. Today's word.

1295.title: Coming back after a lapse
1295.hook: a Sikh who breaks rehat can return through penance and a fresh start
1295.howItsDone: A Sikh who has broken the rehat appears before five amritdhari Sikhs, admits the lapse, and accepts a penance (tankhah); where amrit has been broken, it is taken again. The story of the Mukte of Muktsar is told as a picture of return.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rehat as love: two students, one piece, and a difference only they could hear. Your line was kept in love.

A folded piece of paper. On it, a few lines that say, in effect: you are not our Guru, and we are not your Sikhs. Sikh tradition tells of a band of men from the Majha region who wrote a letter like that during the long siege of Anandpur, signed it, handed it to Guru Gobind Singh, and went home. The word for that letter is bedava, a disclaimer. Tradition says the Guru kept it. You've met the penance the five set when the code is broken. This is about the paper.
screen: `A LETTER: YOU ARE NOT OUR GURU.` → `SIGNED, HANDED OVER, GONE HOME.` → `WHAT HAPPENS TO THE PAPER?`

segments.voice: Here's how the story is told. At home, the men are met with shame instead of welcome. A woman named Mai Bhago, whom you've met before on this path, won't let it rest. Tradition says she rode out with them, back toward the Guru, and they caught up with his pursuers near a pool called Khidrana. They fought there, and they fell. When the Guru came over the field, he found one of them, Mahan Singh, still breathing, and lifted his head into his lap. The dying man asked for one thing: tear up the letter. And the Guru took out the bedava and tore it. Sikhs remember those men as the Mukte, the liberated; the place is called Muktsar, and they're remembered in the Ardas, the prayer said at the close of Sikh gatherings. Now set the code beside the story. The Rehat Maryada says, in paraphrase, that a Sikh who breaks the rehat should come before the five, admit it plainly, accept the penance they set, and, where amrit has been broken, take it again. Then the person begins fresh. As the code lays it out, the procedure is a way back in. The story says the same thing in another key. The men didn't come back by arguing they'd been right. They came back, and gave everything. The paper that said we are not your Sikhs wasn't filed away as evidence. The Guru tore it.
screen: `MAI BHAGO RIDES THEM BACK.` · `THE GURU TEARS THE LETTER.` · `THE CODE: ADMIT, ACCEPT, BEGIN AGAIN.` · then, large: `THE DOOR STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who drifted away, from you, a family, a team, a friendship or a faith community, whether they left loudly or just stopped coming. Hold them without rehearsing the argument, and picture one small, real way to make coming back easier: a message, a seat saved, a plain hello. You don't have to send anything; just let the welcome be ready.

Coming back after a lapse. In the Sikh code, one who breaks rehat comes before the five, accepts a penance, and starts fresh. In the story of Muktsar, the Guru tears up the letter that said goodbye. Today's word.
screen: `COMING BACK AFTER A LAPSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: you can return. The Guru tore the letter. A week ends with an open door.
